title: Law-Enforcement Innovate to De-Escalate Act
official_title: To modernize Federal firearms laws to account for advancements in technology and less-than-lethal weapons, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Fitzgerald (R-WI) with Rep. Correa (D-CA) and 95 cosponsors; passed the House. Broad bipartisan cosponsorship and a narrow, technical scope improve its chances in the Senate, though it has not yet received a Senate vote.
summary: Carves 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' out of federal firearms restrictions and defines what qualifies, so they are not regulated as firearms.
brief: Amends federal firearms law to exempt 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' from regulation and defines the term.

top_lines.headline: Less-Than-Lethal Device Exemption
subs: Exempts 'less-than-lethal projectile devices' from Title 18 firearms rules
Defines the term by velocity (under 500 fps) and design
Attorney General must rule on a device within 90 days

items.main: Names the Act the “Law-Enforcement Innovate to De-Escalate Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Exemption of Certain Less-Than-Lethal Projectile Devices

items.main: Amends the firearms definitions in Section 921(a) of title 18 to exclude 'less-than-lethal projectile devices.'
items.detail: Defines a less-than-lethal projectile device as one not designed (and not readily convertible) to fire common handgun, rifle, or shotgun ammunition or any projectile faster than 500 feet per second, designed to be used in a way not likely to cause death or serious bodily injury, and unable to accept semiautomatic-style ammunition feeding devices. If a person asks the Attorney General to determine whether a device qualifies, the Attorney General must decide within 90 days of receiving the device.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, this bill would rip a dangerous new loophole in the Gun Control Act by changing the definition of firearm throughout the entire criminal code to exclude from coverage certain less-than-lethal but still highly dangerous weapons, such as tasers, which have been identified as a contributing factor in more than 500 deaths throughout the United States of America. Mr. Speaker, this bill would exempt these weapons, which are currently classified as firearms, from all regulations under all Federal firearm laws.

Police already have access to less-than-lethal weapons like tasers. They don't need a change in the law. That is not an excuse for changing the law. This bill expands access to dangerous, prohibited individuals by stripping away Federal safeguards. Tasers may not shoot bullets, but they are still dangerous in the wrong hands. This bill would mean that anyone can buy them without a background check including people convicted of serious violent crimes and domestic abusers with restraining orders against them.

Mrs. McBATH. Mr. Speaker, I yield myself the balance of my time. Mr. Speaker, H.R. 2189 does nothing to help law enforcement, who already uses these weapons in all 50 States. It does not provide any new tools or training that would reduce police shootings or promote the safety of officers or the public. Instead, it makes dangerous weapons widely available to everyone, including those who should not have them. It allows those weapons to be untraceable, undetectable by equipment, and sold to anyone without a background check.

gaps: The bill exempts qualifying devices from Title 18 firearms rules but does not address how state law treats the same devices.
It requires the Attorney General to rule within 90 days of receiving a device but specifies no consequence if that deadline is missed.

I am someone who has been a victim of the abuse of law enforcement, and I just haven't heard my colleagues ever talk about it. I came at this bill skeptically when I looked at it. It turns out the bill itself was pretty much written by a corporation, Axon, that wants to sell a new type of taser.

added: New Title II — "Innovate Less Lethal to De-Escalate Tax Modernization Act" added on top of the original provision
Exempts less-than-lethal projectile devices (and qualifying shells/cartridges) from the firearms and ammunition excise tax under Section 4181 (new IRC 4182(d))
Treasury must publish, and update annually, a list of qualifying less-than-lethal projectile devices
Treasury must publish and annually update a list of non-lethal devices whose projectiles exceed 500 feet per second, plus an annual report to House Ways and Means and Senate Finance
Secretary must rule on manufacturer/producer/importer classification requests within 90 days; requests in the first 180 days treated as received at close of that period
Exempts qualifying less-than-lethal projectile devices from the National Firearms Act via amendment to IRC 5845(a)
Effective date: tax exemption applies to articles sold after enactment
modified: Bill restructured into Title I and Title II; original Section 2 became Section 102 under Title I
